(2006), that both the peak and the endset values in thermal analysis lead to a systematic overestimate of the liquidus in dilute solutions. This can be rationalized by considering the melting of a pure component. The local temperature at the melting front remains at the melting point, however, the peak or end of the heat flow curve is dominated only by heat transfer within the material. This effect diminishes with increased alloying and increased freezing range. There are several standard methods for identification of these points which are all similar in their construction, though, there can be some quantitative differences or differences in suitability for different types of reactions. For this report, the data has been assessed using linear baselines and the common definition of steepest rate of ascent/descent to identify the onset or endset from the intersection. All four points and construction aids are shown in Figure 8. The points reflected on the phase diagram are distilled from numerous measurements from each composition. The identified single point is determined by the median value with the error bar ranges coming from the standard error of a linear model based on heating rate. Since the instrumentation is calibrated for 10 K/min, this is considered the most reliable value; however, there are reasons to perform these same tests at different heating/cooling rates in order to observe trends and to exaggerate features. The fitting routine allows for the inclusion of the data produced at other heating and cooling rates. The calibration methods of any instrument can be quite sophisticated, however, this sophistication requires a great deal of underlying certainty in the assumptions lest the calibration solution could actually lead to greater uncertainty. Since some of these methods for modern instrumentation are proprietary, there can be significant uncertainty in how they actually function. In order to eliminate some of the unknown error due to a “blackbox” method, the calibration used here has been stripped down to an easier to follow methodology. 18 Figure 8: Heating and cooling curves showing melting and solidification peaks of a U-11Mo sample at 25 K/min.
